To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we identified a number of differentially methylated genes in a more invasive sub-population of prostate cancer cells.
we identified a novel set of genes, BMX and SOXT, that are epigenetically reprogrammed during prostate cancer invasion and are associated with a more aggressive tumor phenotype.
we have isolated and characterized a population of prostate cancer cells that display an invasive phenotype and are more tumorgenic compared to the bulk population of prostate cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how epigenetic regulation is involved in the process of invasion and the development of more aggressive sub-populations within a tumor.
identifying epigenetically controlled genes in the invasive population of prostate cancer cells and the potential of their use in the development of new biomarkers.
understanding the molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation of the aggressive sub-population in prostate cancer and the role of epigenetics in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our data suggests that the STAT3 signaling pathway is important for the regulation of the invasive sub-population of prostate cells, and may be a key regulator in prostate cancer progression.
the genes BMX and SOXT are important for invasion in prostate cancer and are regulated through DNA methylation in the invasive prostate cancer cell line.
the invasive population of prostate cancer cells have a distinct epigenetic signature that is different from the non-invasive cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified genes that are epigenetically silenced in a population of cells that are more aggressive and have stem cell properties.

we have identified a number of epigenetically regulated genes in the invasive population of cells that are associated with the IL6/STAT3 signaling pathway, and that these genes are also associated with aggressive metastatic prostate cancer.
we have identified a number of genes that may be important in the regulation of invasion in prostate cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IL-6-STAT3 pathway may be important for the invasive phenotype and may be a therapeutic target for prostate cancer.
the invasive population of cells in prostate cancer are epigenetically distinct from the bulk tumor cells and that these epigenetic changes may be important in prostate cancer progression.
the IL-6/JAK/STAT3 pathway plays a significant role in invasive prostate cancer.
